content: Eclampsia, characterized by the occurrence of seizures in the context of pre-eclampsia, is a rare but severe complication during pregnancy. Various anticonvulsant medications are employed to manage eclamptic seizures and prevent their recurrence. This review specifically evaluates the effects of magnesium sulphate compared to diazepam in the treatment of women diagnosed with eclampsia. The analysis included seven randomized controlled trials involving a total of 1,396 women. Among these, three trials, encompassing 1,030 women, were deemed to be of high quality. The findings demonstrated that magnesium sulphate was associated with a significant reduction in maternal mortality compared to diazepam (risk ratio [RR] 0.59, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.38 to 0.92). Additionally, magnesium sulphate was more effective in reducing the recurrence of seizures (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.55). No significant differences were observed between the two treatments in terms of other measures of maternal morbidity. Similarly, there was no clear difference in perinatal mortality (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.34) or neonatal mortality (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.84) between the groups. However, in the magnesium sulphate group, fewer liveborn infants had an Apgar score below seven at one minute (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.87) and at five minutes (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.90). Additionally, fewer infants in this group required intubation at birth (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.00). There was no significant difference in the rate of admission to a special care nursery (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.05). However, fewer infants in the magnesium sulphate group had a hospital stay exceeding seven days (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.96). In conclusion, the use of magnesium sulphate in women with eclampsia significantly reduces the risk of maternal death and the recurrence of seizures compared to diazepam.
